questions.stem: What is the underlying cause of the magnetic field of a permanent bar magnet?
options: Static positive charge built up at the north pole
The flow of a small electric current along its surface
The motion of charges, chiefly the electrons within its atoms
Magnetic charges stored at the north and south ends
questions.explanation: All magnetic effects come from moving charges. In a permanent magnet, the motion and spin of electrons in many atoms are aligned, so their small fields add. There is no separate magnetic charge, and a bar magnet carries no net static charge or surface current from a supply.

questions.stem: How is the direction of a magnetic field at a point defined?
options: The direction of the force on a positive charge moving through that point
The direction from the nearest south pole towards the nearest north pole
The direction in which the north end of a small compass needle points
The direction in which the south end of a small compass needle points
questions.explanation: The field direction is the way a compass needle's north-seeking end points, so outside a magnet the lines run from north to south. The force on a moving charge is perpendicular to the field, not along it.

questions.stem: A soft iron nail is magnetised while near a strong magnet but loses almost all its magnetism when removed. A steel needle treated the same way stays magnetised. Which description is correct?
options: Soft iron forms a permanent magnet and steel forms a temporary magnet
Both form temporary magnets, but the steel takes longer to lose its magnetism
Neither is magnetised; both were simply attracted by the strong magnet
Soft iron forms a temporary magnet and steel forms a permanent magnet
questions.explanation: Soft iron magnetises easily but its domains fall back out of alignment when the external field is removed, so it is a temporary magnet. Steel holds its alignment and becomes a permanent magnet. This is why electromagnet cores are made of soft iron.

questions.stem: Which change makes a current-carrying coil a stronger electromagnet?
options: Replacing the coil's copper wire with thicker insulation
Spreading the same number of turns over a longer core
Reversing the direction of the current in the coil
Placing a soft iron core inside the coil
questions.explanation: A soft iron core becomes magnetised by the coil's field and greatly strengthens it. More turns per unit length and more current also help. Spreading the turns out weakens the field, and reversing the current only swaps the poles.

questions.stem: A compass needle's north-seeking end points towards Earth's geographic North Pole. What kind of magnetic pole lies near the geographic North Pole?
options: No pole; the field there is horizontal
A magnetic north pole that wanders south each year
questions.explanation: Opposite poles attract, so the north end of a compass is pulled towards a magnetic south pole. Earth's field lines therefore enter the ground near the geographic North Pole and leave it near the geographic South Pole.

questions.stem: What is the angle of dip at a place on Earth?
options: The angle between Earth's rotation axis and its magnetic axis
The angle between Earth's magnetic field and the horizontal
The angle between magnetic north and geographic north
The angle between Earth's magnetic field and the vertical
questions.explanation: A dip needle pivoted to swing in a vertical plane shows the angle of dip, the angle of the field below or above the horizontal. The angle between magnetic and geographic north is a different quantity, called declination.

questions.stem: A dip needle in Hobart is free to swing in a vertical north-south plane. Which way does its north-seeking end point?
questions.explanation: In the southern hemisphere Earth's field lines emerge from the ground and head north, because the magnetic pole near the geographic South Pole is a north pole. The needle lines up with the field, so its north end points north and tilts upward, and its south end dips down.

questions.stem: At a certain place, Earth's magnetic field is 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ T at a dip angle of 70°. What is the horizontal component of the field?
questions.explanation: The dip angle is measured from the horizontal, so the horizontal component is B cos 70° = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.342 ≈ 2.1 × 10⁻⁵ T. Using sin 70° gives the vertical component, 5.6 × 10⁻⁵ T. A component can never exceed the full field, which rules out 1.7 × 10⁻⁴ T.

questions.stem: What is the shape of the magnetic field around a long straight wire carrying a steady current?
options: Straight lines running parallel to the wire
Straight lines radiating outward from the wire
Loops that leave one end of the wire and enter the other
Circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it
questions.explanation: The field lines are concentric circles around the wire, and their direction is given by the right-hand grip rule: thumb along the current, fingers curl the way the field circulates. Radiating lines describe the electric field of a charged wire.

questions.stem: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. What is the magnetic flux density 5.0 cm from the wire? Use k = 2 × 10⁻⁷ N A⁻².
questions.explanation: B = kI/r = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 10 / 0.050 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T. Leaving the distance in centimetres gives 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ T, and dividing by r² instead of r gives 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ T.

questions.stem: The magnetic flux density at a certain distance from a long straight wire is B. What is it at twice that distance?
questions.explanation: For a straight wire B = kI/r, so B is inversely proportional to the distance. Doubling r halves B. A factor of one-quarter would apply to an inverse square law such as the field of a point charge.

questions.stem: A horizontal wire carries a current due north. What is the direction of its magnetic field at a point directly below the wire?
questions.explanation: With the right thumb pointing north along the current, the fingers curl from east over the top of the wire to west underneath it. So the field below the wire points west, and above the wire it points east. The field is never along the current.

questions.stem: Two long parallel wires 0.20 m apart carry currents of 6.0 A and 4.0 A in the same direction. What is the magnetic flux density midway between them? Use k = 2 × 10⁻⁷ N A⁻².
questions.explanation: Each wire is 0.10 m away. The 6.0 A wire gives 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ T and the 4.0 A wire gives 8.0 × 10⁻⁶ T. With currents in the same direction, the two fields point in opposite directions between the wires, so the net field is the difference, 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ T. Adding them gives 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ T; zero would need equal currents.

questions.stem: Two long straight wires cross at right angles in the plane of the page. One carries 5.0 A to the east and the other 8.0 A to the north. Point P is 0.10 m north of the east-west wire and 0.20 m east of the north-south wire. What is the magnetic flux density at P? Use k = 2 × 10⁻⁷ N A⁻².
questions.explanation: The east-west wire gives 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 5.0 / 0.10 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ T, out of the page at P by the grip rule. The north-south wire gives 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 8.0 / 0.20 = 8.0 × 10⁻⁶ T, into the page at P. Both fields are perpendicular to the page, so they subtract, leaving 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ T out of the page. Adding them gives 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ T.

questions.stem: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. What force do they exert on each other?
options: They exert no force on each other
They twist each other to lie at right angles
questions.explanation: Each wire sits in the other's magnetic field and experiences a force. For currents in the same direction the forces pull the wires together; for opposite currents they push the wires apart. This is the opposite of the rule for like and unlike charges.

questions.stem: Two parallel wires, each 2.0 m long, are 0.10 m apart and each carries 5.0 A. What is the force between them? Use k = 2 × 10⁻⁷ N A⁻².
questions.explanation: F = kI₁I₂l/r = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 5.0 × 5.0 × 2.0 / 0.10 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ N. Leaving out the length gives 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ N, the force per metre. Dividing by r² gives 1.0 × 10⁻³ N.

questions.stem: The currents in two parallel wires are both doubled while the separation stays the same. By what factor does the force between them change?
options: It increases by a factor of two
It decreases by a factor of four
It increases by a factor of four
questions.explanation: The force is proportional to the product I₁I₂. Doubling both currents multiplies the product by 2 × 2 = 4. Doubling only one current would double the force.

questions.stem: Wire X carries 2.0 A and wire Y, parallel to it, carries 6.0 A. How does the force on X compare with the force on Y?
options: The force on X is three times the force on Y
The force on Y is three times the force on X
The force on Y is nine times the force on X
They are equal in size and opposite in direction
questions.explanation: The forces form a Newton's third law pair, so they are equal and opposite. Both depend on the product I₁I₂, so neither wire feels a larger force, even though Y's own field is stronger.

questions.stem: Which statement defines a magnetic flux density of 1 tesla?
options: A field in which a 1 m wire carrying 1 A at right angles to it feels a force of 1 N
A field in which a 1 C charge at rest feels a force of 1 N
A field produced 1 m from a long straight wire carrying a current of 1 A
A field in which a 1 m wire moving at 1 m s⁻¹ has an emf of 1 J
questions.explanation: From B = F/(Il sin θ), 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹. A charge at rest feels no magnetic force at all, and the field 1 m from a 1 A wire is only 2 × 10⁻⁷ T.

questions.stem: A 0.25 m length of wire carrying 3.0 A lies at right angles to a uniform 0.40 T magnetic field. What force acts on it?
questions.explanation: F = BIl sin θ = 0.40 × 3.0 × 0.25 × sin 90° = 0.30 N. Dividing by the length instead of multiplying gives 4.8 N, dividing by the current gives 0.033 N, and 0.15 N would apply only at 30° to the field.

questions.stem: The same 0.25 m wire carrying 3.0 A is turned so that it makes an angle of 30° with the 0.40 T field. What force acts on it now?
questions.explanation: F = BIl sin θ, where θ is the angle between wire and field: 0.40 × 3.0 × 0.25 × sin 30° = 0.15 N. Using cos 30° gives 0.26 N, the value for a wire at 60° to the field, and dividing by sin 30° gives 0.60 N.

questions.stem: A straight wire carrying a current lies parallel to a uniform magnetic field. What magnetic force acts on it?
options: BIl/2, at right angles to the wire
BIl, at right angles to the wire
questions.explanation: F = BIl sin θ and θ = 0° for a wire parallel to the field, so sin θ = 0 and there is no force. The force is greatest when the wire is perpendicular to the field.

questions.stem: A horizontal wire carries a current to the east through a horizontal magnetic field pointing north. What is the direction of the force on the wire?
questions.explanation: Using the right-hand palm rule with fingers north for the field and thumb east for the current, the palm pushes upward. The force is always perpendicular to both the current and the field, so it cannot be north or west.

questions.stem: A horizontal wire 0.20 m long with a mass of 6.0 g lies at right angles to a horizontal 0.50 T field. What current makes the magnetic force exactly balance its weight? Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².
questions.explanation: For balance, BIl = mg, so I = mg/(Bl) = 0.0060 × 9.81 / (0.50 × 0.20) ≈ 0.59 A. Leaving the mass in grams gives 590 A, leaving out g gives 0.060 A, and multiplying by Bl instead of dividing gives 0.0059 A.

questions.stem: What is the job of the split-ring commutator in a simple DC motor?
options: To keep the current in the coil flowing the same way at all times
To change the direct current from the supply into alternating current at the brushes
To reduce the current in the coil when it spins too fast
To reverse the current in the coil every half turn so it keeps turning one way
questions.explanation: Without the commutator the forces on the coil would reverse the turning effect after each half turn and the coil would rock back and forth. Reversing the current in the coil every half turn keeps the torque in one direction.

questions.stem: A rectangular motor coil has 20 turns. Each side cutting the field is 0.050 m long, the current is 2.0 A and the field is 0.30 T. What is the force on one side of the coil when it is perpendicular to the field?
questions.explanation: Each turn contributes BIl, so the force on one side is nBIl = 20 × 0.30 × 2.0 × 0.050 = 0.60 N. Leaving out the number of turns gives 0.030 N, and 1.2 N counts both sides, which push in opposite directions.

questions.stem: In a simple DC motor, at which position of the coil is the turning effect zero?
options: When the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field
When the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field
When the plane of the coil is at 45° to the magnetic field
When the current in the coil is at its largest
questions.explanation: With the coil's plane perpendicular to the field, the forces on the two sides still act but point along the plane of the coil, through the axle, so they produce no torque. With the plane parallel to the field the forces are perpendicular to the plane and the torque is greatest.

questions.stem: A motor coil is turned so that its plane is parallel to the magnetic field. What force acts on the two short ends of the coil that run parallel to the field?
options: Zero, because the current in them is parallel to the field
The largest possible force, because they are at the edge of the field
A force along their length, pushing them apart
A force equal to that on the long sides of the coil
questions.explanation: The ends of the coil carry current parallel or antiparallel to the field, so sin θ = 0 and F = BIl sin θ = 0. Only the sides perpendicular to the field feel a force in this position.

questions.stem: Why does the magnetic force on a moving charged particle not change its speed?
options: The force is too small compared with the particle's momentum to change its speed
The force acts only while the particle is entering the field
The force is always perpendicular to the particle's velocity, so it does no work
The force is always parallel to the particle's velocity, so it only changes direction
questions.explanation: F = qvB acts at right angles to the velocity. A force perpendicular to the motion does no work, so the kinetic energy and speed stay constant and only the direction changes. This is why the particle moves in a circle.

questions.stem: A proton moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a 0.50 T magnetic field. What magnetic force acts on it?
questions.explanation: F = qvB = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁶ × 0.50 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N. Dividing by B instead of multiplying gives 6.4 × 10⁻¹³ N, and using the proton's mass in place of its charge gives 1.7 × 10⁻²¹ N.

questions.stem: An electron moves due north through a magnetic field that points vertically downward. What is the direction of the magnetic force on it?
questions.explanation: For a positive charge, the right-hand palm rule with thumb north and fingers down gives a force to the west. An electron is negative, so the force on it is reversed, to the east. The force is always perpendicular to both the velocity and the field.

questions.stem: A proton travels at 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform 0.20 T field. What is the radius of its circular path? Use a proton mass of 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
questions.explanation: r = mv/(qB) = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × 3.0 × 10⁶ / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.20) ≈ 0.16 m. Using the electron's mass gives 8.5 × 10⁻⁵ m, and 6.4 m comes from inverting the fraction.

questions.stem: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at 40° to the field lines. What path does it follow?
options: A straight line, since only charges moving perpendicular to a field feel a force
A helix around the field lines, since the velocity component along the field is unchanged
A circle, since the magnetic force is perpendicular to its velocity
A parabola, since the magnetic force is constant in size and direction
questions.explanation: Only the velocity component perpendicular to the field, v sin θ, produces a force, which turns it into circular motion of radius mv sin θ/(qB). The component along the field is unaffected, so the circle is stretched into a helix. This is how charged particles spiral along Earth's field lines in the Van Allen belts.

questions.stem: A charged particle moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is doubled, what happens to the radius of its path?
options: It increases by a factor of four
questions.explanation: r = mv/(qB), so the radius is directly proportional to speed. A faster particle has more momentum and is turned less sharply by the same field.

questions.stem: An electron and a proton enter the same uniform magnetic field at the same speed, at right angles to the field. How do their paths compare?
options: The electron's circle is much smaller and curves the opposite way
The electron's circle is much larger and curves the opposite way
The circles are the same size and curve the opposite way
The electron's circle is much smaller and curves the same way
questions.explanation: The charges have equal size but opposite sign, so the forces are opposite and the paths curve in opposite senses. Since r = mv/(qB) and the electron's mass is about 1/1840 of the proton's, its radius is far smaller.

questions.stem: In a velocity filter, a uniform electric field of 3.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ is crossed with a uniform magnetic field of 0.15 T. At what speed do ions pass straight through?
questions.explanation: An ion passes undeflected when the electric and magnetic forces balance: qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 3.0 × 10⁴ / 0.15 = 2.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Multiplying gives 4.5 × 10³, and B/E gives 5.0 × 10⁻⁶. The charge cancels, so the selected speed is the same for every ion.

questions.stem: In a velocity filter set to pass ions of speed E/B undeflected, an ion enters moving faster than E/B. What happens to it?
options: It passes straight through, but only if it carries a single positive charge
It is deflected in the direction of the magnetic force, which now exceeds the electric force
It is deflected in the direction of the electric force, which now exceeds the magnetic force
It passes straight through, because both forces increase in the same ratio
questions.explanation: The electric force qE does not depend on speed, but the magnetic force qvB grows with speed. A faster ion feels a magnetic force larger than the electric force, so it is pushed towards the magnetic force's side and blocked by the exit slit.

questions.stem: Singly charged neon-20 and neon-22 ions leave a velocity filter at 2.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ and enter a 0.50 T field in a Bainbridge mass spectrometer. They travel half circles to a detector. How far apart do they land? Use 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
questions.explanation: r = mv/(qB) gives 0.0830 m for neon-20 and 0.0913 m for neon-22. Each ion lands one diameter from the entry slit, so the separation is 2 × (0.0913 − 0.0830) ≈ 0.017 m. Stopping at the difference in radii gives 0.83 cm, and 8.3 cm is the radius of the neon-20 path.
